title: Arjuna drops his bow
hook: a warrior sits down in his chariot, and the line Krishna answers with
carry: your right is to the act, never its fruit
tomorrow: one bar, one word. except when it isn't. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole week came back in half of Nani's line: karma yoga, act fully, offer the fruit. Now the whole line, and the story it comes from. It starts with a mark that isn't a letter at all.

At a kitchen table, a granddaughter is copying her grandmother's favorite line into a birthday card. Halfway through, after the word kadachana, she finds a stick standing on its own. At the end, two sticks, with the verse number tucked between them. That first stick isn't the number one. It's a danda, a staff, Devanagari's stop: one stroke for half a verse, two when the verse is whole. And this verse has two halves for a reason. It comes from a moment when a man stopped halfway.
screen: `A STICK HALFWAY THROUGH NANI'S LINE.` → `THE DANDA: A STOP.` → `A VERSE IN TWO HALVES.`

segments.voice: The man is Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, standing in a chariot between two armies on the field of Kurukshetra. Krishna holds the reins. Arjuna asks him to drive into the middle so he can see who he has to fight, and he sees them: his teachers, his great-uncle Bhishma, cousins, friends. His mouth goes dry. His bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand. He sits down in the chariot and says, I will not fight. Krishna's answer is the Bhagavad Gita, and in its second chapter comes the line in the card. The first half, up to the single danda: your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. Then a breath. The second half shuts a door Arjuna was hoping to walk through: don't make the fruit your reason for acting, and don't cling to not acting either. Two dandas. Whole. This is the heart of what Hindus call karma yoga: do what your dharma asks, fully, and let go of your claim on how it turns out. Not 'don't care.' Arjuna is told to care enough to act, and to stop needing the result to be his. Many teachers read the second half as the sharpest part: fear of how it will turn out is no reason to put the bow down. That may be why a grandmother loves this line. A long life holds a lot of moments where the result was never in her hands, and the work still was.
screen: `ARJUNA'S BOW SLIPS.` · `I WILL NOT FIGHT.` · `FIRST HALF: THE ACT IS YOURS, NEVER THE FRUIT.` · `SECOND HALF: DON'T HIDE IN NOT ACTING.` · `KARMA YOGA.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you have to do today whose outcome isn't up to you. On each in-breath, name the act, the part that's yours. On each out-breath, set the result down; if you pray, offer it to God, as Krishna asks Arjuna to; many Hindus say it in two words, Krishnarpanam astu, may it be offered to Krishna. Stay with it, breath after breath: the act held, the fruit let go.
Devanagari: the script that holds Nani's line, with one danda at the half-way breath and two at the end.
Your line: your right is to the act, never its fruit. Arjuna is still sitting in the chariot. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Printed Sanskrit verse usually closes its first half with a single danda (।) and the full verse with a double danda (॥), often with the verse number between; Bhagavad Gita 2.47 is widely quoted and often taught as the core of karma yoga.

original.note: Sanskrit: the discipline of action: doing your duty and letting go of the fruit.

what it means: Krishna tells Arjuna the act is his and the fruit is not, and that fear of the fruit is no reason to stop acting.
what a scholar hears: Gita 2.47's two halves, split by the danda: a right to action only, never its fruits; then no clinging to inaction. the root of karma yoga.

chat.meaning: Arjuna dropped his bow and refused to act. Krishna told him his right is to the act, never its fruits, and not to cling to not acting. That's karma yoga.

tie.story: Arjuna put down his bow, and Krishna told him the act was his to do, never the fruit his to hold.

danda.meaning: a staff; the upright stroke that ends a sentence or half-verse

kadachana.meaning: ever, at any time; with ma, 'never'

Gita.meaning: the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna

Arjuna.meaning: the archer prince Krishna teaches in the Gita

Kurukshetra.meaning: the battlefield where the Gita is spoken

dharma.meaning: duty, what is right for you to do
